Title: 

It is the first time since October 2024 that the right-wing party has polled in the teens, according to the new survey. It comes as Reform’s home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf says that former Tories who defected to the party cannot be trusted on immigration

It is the first time since October 2024 that the right-wing party has polled in the teens, according to the new survey. It comes as Reform’s home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf says that former Tories who defected to the party cannot be trusted on immigration

BookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarks

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The crisis for Nigel Farage has deepened after his party dropped below 20 per cent in a poll for the first time in more than two years.

According to More in Common, Reform UK is on 19 per cent – the first time since October 2024 that it has polled in the teens. It is a long fall from Reform’s high of 33 per cent in another More in Common poll in late October 2025.

The drop comes despite Mr Farage’s attempts to clean up his party’s image and is 11 points down from the 30 per cent it was at this time last year.

Last week, he brought in Angus McIntyre, a recently retired wing commander who worked with Nato and Ukraine, in an apparent effort to show his party is not pro-Russia. But the party has been on a downward trajectory since questions were asked about a £5m donation made to Mr Farage by crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne which went undeclared and is under investigation by the standards commissioner.

Police are investigating former chief of staff Dan Jukes and former policy director James Orr after Channel 4 revealed they may have been willing to accept illegal donations.

Meanwhile, there have been problems over candidate selections with an ITV documentary exposing racism and misogyny.

Added to that, internal party tensions remain, with recent barbed remarks by home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf about leading former Tory defectors Suella Braverman and Robert Jenrick.

Recently, former home secretary Ms Braverman denied she was being referred to by Mr Yusuf when he said: “Top tip: If you meet someone and their title is ‘Right Honourable’, assume they are the most dishonourable person you have ever met.” Then he doubled down by saying that former Tories – including Ms Braverman and Mr Jenrick – who jumped ship to Reform had been barred from shaping the party’s immigration and culture policies.

He said: “If you are in the category of being concerned about (former Tories), none of the above are going to be involved in immigration policy or borders policy. There’s a reason why Nigel’s given me this brief and not them.”

The More in Common poll showed Labour up one point to 29 per cent and the Tories six points ahead of Reform on 25 per cent. There were poor showings for the Lib Dems on 9 per cent and Greens on 8 per cent, both of whom appear to be struggling since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common, said: “Labour is at its joint highest score since we resumed polling after the election. Reform has now declined 11 points since the aftermath of the local elections in May 2025, and the Conservatives are up six points.”

Noting that public opinion of the party leaders is also hitting new lows, he added: “[Green leader Zack] Polanski (-37), Farage (-34), and [Restore leader Rupert] Lowe (-22) all hit their lowest ever net approval scores in our tracker, with [Lib Dem leader] Ed Davey (-14) also falling to his joint low. Meanwhile, [Tory leader Kemi] Badenoch’s approval is down to net neutral, and Burnham’s is down to +8.”

Stripping out negative views of the leaders, the leadership table is also reflected on gross approval ratings. Mr Burnham leads, at 40 per cent, followed by Ms Badenoch at 35 per cent, Mr Farage at 23 per cent, Mr Davey at 18 per cent, Mr Polanski at 14 per cent and Mr Lowe at 14 per cent.

Mr Farage will try to reverse his party’s downward spiral by launching a new pro-Brexit campaign in Brussels on Friday. The launch will take place as Mr Burnham signs the latest Brexit reset deal with a view that it will be a launchpad for a much more radical overhaul of Britain’s status with the EU.
